The deepsea brittlestar Ophiomusa lymani is a bathyal ophiuroid that undergoes a pelagic planktotrophic larval phase before settling to the seafloor. Following broadcast fertilisation, the resulting yolk-dependent embryo develops within a small transparent egg possessing an estimated diameter of 0.46 millimeters, which yields a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00005 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00005 grams]. Hatched ophiopluteus larvae drift in the water column for a period of about 2 days [ab = about 2 days] when maintained at a stable bottom-water temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C], a developmental duration that closely mirrors the abbreviated larval phase reported for the congeners Amphiura filiformis. During the metamorphic climax, the bilateral pluteus body plan undergoes a dramatic allometric shift and arm resorption, leading to the formation of a post-metamorphic juvenile characterised by a disc diameter at metamorphosis of 0.0325 centimeters . This tiny newly recruited individual resembles a miniature adult, initiating a prolonged benthic existence that will span many years under the cold, food-limited conditions of the deep-sea environment.

Post-settlement growth in Ophiomusa lymani proceeds slowly, a pattern consistent with the low metabolic and temperature regime typical of abyssal habitats. The growing juvenile eventually reaches sexual maturity, signalled by the onset of gametogenesis, when its disc attains a diameter of 2 centimeters [Lp = 2 centimeters]. Achieving puberty requires that the disc diameter reach 2 centimeters [Lp = 2 centimeters], a size representing approximately 74 percent of the ultimate adult disc diameter (2.7 centimeters) [Li = 2.7 centimeters], and one that is not attained until several years after settlement. At this same life stage, the individual has accumulated a corresponding ash-free dry weight at puberty of approximately 0.21 grams , a value derived from the scaling relationship between linear and mass dimensions within this species. Reaching this developmental milestone requires several years of steady feeding on organic detritus and small benthic invertebrates, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by the chronically cold and food-poor deep-sea environment where these brittlestars reside.

As individuals continue to age, their disc diameter expands until it approaches an asymptotic upper limit. The ultimate disc diameter for this species is 2.7 centimeters [Li = 2.7 centimeters], a maximum recorded size that is rarely observed in field collections, likely because mortality intervenes before many individuals attain this theoretically maximal dimension. Coinciding with this maximal linear dimension is the ultimate ash-free dry weight, which reaches 0.511 grams  in the largest, most reproductively active adults. This mass value, corresponding to the fully grown state, provides a benchmark for evaluating the energetic investment that mature females can divert toward spawning each year. Under the cold thermal conditions characteristic of the bathyal zone, a stable 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C] environment, estimates of the maximum reproduction rate indicate that females can produce, on a daily basis, approximately 33 eggs [Ri = daily basis, approximately 33 eggs], a rate that translates into substantial annual fecundity. This considerable fecundity is a typical life-history adaptation among deep-sea echinoderms, offsetting the extremely low survival probabilities faced by their planktonic larvae in the dilute, unproductive waters of the deep ocean.

The species' lifespan is constrained by the same cold temperatures that govern its developmental and reproductive schedule. At a constant ambient temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C], the maximum recorded longevity in Ophiomusa lymani is 3 years [am = 3 years], a relatively short duration for a deep-sea organism and one that is somewhat shorter than that reported for certain other bathyal ophiuroids of comparable body size. Field observations suggest that individuals rarely exceed 36 months [am = 36 months], a lifespan that appears to be tightly coupled to the low metabolic rates imposed by persistent cold temperatures at a temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]. Senescence and natural mortality follow the final spawning bouts, with few individuals surviving beyond their third year. The interplay between a short adult phase and a high per-capita fecundity underscores a bet-hedging strategy that stabilises population persistence despite stochastic recruitment success in the variable deep-sea environment.

The reproductive output of Ophiomusa lymani, partitioned across multiple spawning events each year, is remarkably high for a deep-sea ophiuroid of its body size. An annual fecundity of approximately 12,000 eggsnan, produced over a maximum lifespan of just 3 years [am = 3 years], yields a lifetime fecundity that may exceed 36,000 eggs per female at a temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]. This prodigious per capita investment reflects a classical r-selected strategy within an overall K-selected environment: the species offsets extremely high larval mortality in the oligotrophic deep sea by flooding the water column with large numbers of small, planktotrophic larvae. The tiny disc diameter at metamorphosis of 0.0325 centimeters  underscores the vulnerability of newly settled juveniles, which must immediately commence feeding on scarce organic particles to sustain growth toward the 2-centimeter disc diameter (2 centimeters) [Lp = 2 centimeters] required for reproductive maturity. This combination of high fecundity, abbreviated larval development, and moderate adult size exemplifies the adaptive suite that enables Ophiomusa lymani to persist in the challenging bathyal environment.
